item.text:
**Reused evidence**
- `E0004` and `E0105` cover the stated program and formal implementation structure, especially `8B.1`, `8B.2`, `8B.3`, `8B.6`, `8B.10`.
- `E0069`, `E0070`, `E0073`, `E0074`, `E0076`, `E0077`, `E0078`, `E0111` cover war-economy outcomes and constraints, mainly `8B.7`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.
- `E0082` and `E0089` cover official social/health delivery claims, mainly `8B.2`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.10`.
- `E0101` and `E0102` cover top-level personnel changes and loyalist placement, mainly `8B.4`, `8B.5`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.

**New evidence**
- **Russian Federation (country profile, 2024)**, WHO Europe, **2024-11-25**, https://www.who.int/europe/ru/publications/m/item/health-impact-2024-rus-country-profile. Claim: WHO says Russia used SAFER-type alcohol controls, piloted RUS-AUDIT in primary care, and saw TB incidence/deaths decline; source type is a WHO country technical document, high credibility but program-level and not an audit of Putin personally. Temporal fit: direct 2024 profile. Attribution and limits: shows independent health-system output and outcome trends under Putin-era governance, but not direct proof of Putin’s personal management. Contrary points: aggregate, partially self-reported system performance, not a 2024 service-quality audit. Lenses: `8B.2`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.10`.

- **Russian Federation (RUS) - Demographics, Health & Infant Mortality**, UNICEF DATA, latest page crawl 2024, https://data.unicef.org/country/rus/. Claim: under-five mortality was **5.2** in 2024; DTP3 coverage **97**; measles coverage **93**; safely managed sanitation **58**; safely managed drinking water **76**. Source type is UNICEF country data, high credibility for independent outcome measurement. Temporal fit: strongest on 2024 mortality and coverage metrics. Attribution and limits: country-level outcome indicators, not direct ruler attribution; long-run institutional and regional factors remain confounders. Contrary points: some service-access indicators are available while others are not, so quality and equity remain only partly visible. Lenses: `8B.7`, `8B.10`, with indirect support for `8B.2` and `8B.6`.

- **Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation**, UNICEF DATA, latest page crawl 2024, https://data.unicef.org/sdgs/country/rus/. Claim: Russia shows under-five mortality **5** (2021), neonatal mortality **2** (2021), skilled-birth attendance **100%** (2020), child poverty below the national line **12%** (2020), and child social protection coverage **100%** (2020). Source type is UNICEF SDG country tracking, high credibility but lagged. Temporal fit: indirect for 2024, but still a useful independent benchmark. Attribution and limits: these are not direct Putin-program audits, and several values are older than 2024. Contrary points: UNICEF itself flags data gaps for some child-wellbeing measures. Lenses: `8B.7`, `8B.10`, with indirect support for `8B.2` and `8B.6`.

- **In Focus: Ending child poverty**, UNICEF Europe and Central Asia, **2024-11**, https://www.unicef.org/eca/reports/focus-ending-child-poverty-2024. Claim: Russia had the region’s largest increase in children living in poverty, with an additional **2.8 million** children below the poverty line; UNICEF also says child benefits in the region were not consistently reducing poverty. Source type is a strong independent regional UNICEF analysis. Temporal fit: late-2024, but regionwide rather than Putin-specific. Attribution and limits: useful contrary evidence on social distribution and measurement limits, but not a direct Russian national program evaluation. Contrary points: the report also says child-poverty measurement is often incomplete, so the negative signal is real but not fully precise. Lenses: `8B.7`, `8B.10`.

- **Russian Federation | Data**, World Bank, latest page crawl 2025 with 2023/2024 values, https://data.worldbank.org/country/RU. Claim: life expectancy at birth was **73** in 2023; poverty headcount at $3/day was **0.1%** in 2023; population was **143,533,851** in 2024/2025 display. Source type is independent global development data, high credibility. Temporal fit: one-year lag on some indicators. Attribution and limits: country-level outcomes, not Putin-specific proof. Contrary points: does not resolve distributional or service-quality questions by itself. Lenses: `8B.7`, `8B.10`.

- **Back in Stock? The State of Russia's Defense Industry after Two Years of the War**, CSIS, **2024-04-22**, https://www.csis.org/analysis/back-stock-state-russias-defense-industry-after-two-years-war. Claim: the report examines Russia’s “evolving defense industrial capabilities and limitations” and how they affect battlefield outcomes in Ukraine. Source type is a high-credibility independent defense analysis. Temporal fit: strong for 2024. Attribution and limits: helps distinguish war-economy output from ruler skill, but it still uses open-source inference rather than direct Kremlin internal audit. Contrary points: the report stresses both capability gains and limitations, so it does not read as a simple competence endorsement. Lenses: `8B.3`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.

- **Russian Military Objectives and Capacity in Ukraine Through 2024**, RUSI, 2024 commentary, https://www.rusi.org/explore-our-research/publications/commentary/russian-military-objectives-and-capacity-ukraine-through-2024?wpappninja_v=an583vqgw. Claim: Russia could sustain a steady tempo of attacks through 2024; recruiters were achieving about **85%** of targets, industrial output included roughly **1,500 tanks per year** and about **3,000 AFVs**, but ammunition requirements still exceeded expected production. Source type is a strong independent military analysis with explicit quantitative estimates. Temporal fit: direct 2024. Attribution and limits: useful for implementation and adaptation, but the numbers are still open-source estimates and not a Kremlin audit. Contrary points: the same source says ammunition shortages and supplier dependence remain serious. Lenses: `8B.3`, `8B.5`, `8B.7`, `8B.8`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.

- **Russian think tank warns of stagnating industrial output, investment**, Reuters via Investing.com, **2024-04-27**, https://www.investing.com/news/economy/russian-think-tank-warns-of-stagnating-industrial-output-investment-3401936. Claim: a government-close think tank said Russian industrial production and investment were stagnating, exports were deteriorating, profitability was declining, and imported-component shortages persisted. Source type is Reuters reporting on a domestic think tank, high credibility but second-order. Temporal fit: direct 2024. Attribution and limits: valuable contrary evidence on the economic side, but still not a pure Putin-competence audit. Contrary points: it undercuts any simple “war mobilization solved the economy” story. Lenses: `8B.7`, `8B.9`, `8B.10`.

**Search and rejection summary**
- Considered roughly 20 documents across WHO, UNICEF, World Bank, CSIS, RUSI, IISS, Reuters, and the existing evidence index.
- Rejected as duplicates or near-duplicates: mirrored Reuters syndications on Investing/ThePrint for the same defense-production and personnel stories, plus overlapping current-index items already covering the same program and wartime execution chain.
- Rejected as weak for this gap: generic global UNICEF annual reports, older background-only World Bank material, and Kremlin/government self-reporting that does not independently verify outcomes.
- Blockers: the UNICEF child-poverty page had a cache miss on direct open, so I used the stable search snippet; the RUSI commentary’s quantitative section was not fully exposed in open view, so I relied on the searchable snippet text.

**Remaining gaps**
| Gap | Status | What remains |
|---|---|---|
| Independent measures of some social and health outcomes are weaker than official reporting | Partly resolved | WHO/UNICEF/World Bank now provide independent outcome data, but a direct 2024 audit of service quality, delivery fidelity, and region-by-region variation is still not recoverable from open sources. |
| Causal attribution of economic and military outcomes to Putin’s own competence is confounded by war economy, force size, and inherited capacity | Partly resolved | CSIS, RUSI, Reuters, and IISS show real mobilization and real constraints, but the precise share due to Putin’s own competence versus structural inputs remains not recoverable. |
